topic_summary: The Medicare Levy Surcharge (MLS) applies to Australian taxpayers who earn above the singles threshold of $101,000 or the family threshold of $202,000 (plus $1,500 per dependent child after the first) and do not hold appropriate private patient hospital cover. The MLS is levied at 1%, 1.25%, or 1.5% on top of the Medicare levy, is not withheld by employers, and is calculated at tax return time. Spouse status, dependants, and mid-year changes in circumstances all affect liability.

terminals.heading: I'm single — do I have to pay the MLS?
terminals.result_copy: Your indicated income for MLS purposes is at or below the $101,000 singles base income threshold for 2025–26. Review recommended: the mls-do-i-pay-single dish explains how 'income for MLS purposes' is calculated and how to confirm your position using the ATO Income tax estimator — no definite outcome is asserted here.

terminals.heading: I have a spouse or dependants — how does the family threshold work?
terminals.result_copy: Your indicated family income for MLS purposes is at or below the $202,000 family base income threshold (plus $1,500 for each dependent child after the first) for 2025–26, or your own income for MLS purposes was $27,222 or less while you had a spouse for the full year. Review recommended: the mls-do-i-pay-family dish explains how the family threshold works and how to confirm your position — no definite outcome is asserted here.

terminals.heading: I have private hospital cover — am I exempt from the MLS?
terminals.result_copy: You have indicated you hold (or may hold) private patient hospital cover. Review recommended: not all policies qualify as 'appropriate' cover for MLS exemption purposes. The mls-exempt-private-cover dish explains what the policy must cover and flags considerations such as waiting periods and exclusions — no definite exemption outcome is asserted here.

terminals.heading: What counts as 'income for MLS purposes'?
terminals.result_copy: Income for Medicare levy surcharge purposes is not the same as your taxable income. It is the sum of your taxable income (including any net amount on which family trust distribution tax has been paid), reportable fringe benefits, total net investment losses — both net financial investment losses and net rental property losses — reportable super contributions (employer contributions plus deductible personal contributions), a spouse's share of certain trust income taxed to the trustee, and exempt foreign employment income. If you negatively gear a property, this figure is HIGHER than your taxable income, not lower — which is how people who believe they are under the threshold turn out to be over it. If you have a spouse, the ATO uses your combined income for MLS purposes. Source: ATO QC49961. No definite income figure or MLS outcome is asserted here.

terminals.heading: My circumstances changed mid-year (new spouse, separation, or cover cancelled) — what happens?
terminals.result_copy: Your circumstances changed during 2025–26. Review recommended: the mls-mid-year-change-circumstances dish explains how mid-year changes affect MLS liability on a pro-rata (number of days) basis and how to report these changes in your tax return — no definite outcome is asserted here.

terminals.heading: Why wasn't the MLS taken out of my pay — and what do I owe at tax time?
terminals.result_copy: Your income for MLS purposes appears to exceed the applicable threshold and you do not have appropriate cover. terminals.heading: The Medicare levy surcharge may not apply to your situation
terminals.result_copy: Your answers suggest this check may not fit — for example you are not an Australian resident for tax purposes, or your circumstances are not described by any of the household situations above. If you do earn above the singles threshold of $101,000 or the family threshold of $202,000 for 2025–26 and do not hold appropriate private patient hospital cover, the surcharge is likely to apply — a short personalised review confirms whether it does and what it would cost you.
